t: LeetCode 1682 — Longest Palindromic Subsequence II: Build Pairs From the Edges With a Banned Neighbor Letter
o:
A "good" palindromic subsequence must be an even-length palindrome whose adjacent characters all differ except the middle pair - "abba" qualifies, "bcb" fails (odd length), "bbbb" fails (equal neighbors). So the shape is forced: choose symmetric pairs of equal letters from the outside inward; every newly chosen inner pair must use a letter different from the pair wrapping it, and the innermost pair supplies the one exempt equal middle.

Example 1: bbabab hides "baab" (outer pair b, middle pair a) for length 4. Example 2: dcbccacdb yields "dccd", also length 4.

With n up to 250, an O(26 x n^2) interval DP over states (window, letter banned next to the boundary) is the natural target complexity.
k: Building from the edges reduces the state to (left, right, lastPairLetter); the next inner pair must avoid that letter.
For a fixed window and pair letter, anchoring on the leftmost and rightmost occurrences maximizes the interior window, hence the value.
Even length means characters are consumed in pairs only - a lone unmatched center character contributes nothing.

a.n: Approach 1: Top-Down DFS with Memo on (l, r, prev)
a.i: dfs(l, r, prev) answers: inside window s[l..r], what is the longest good palindrome whose next outer pair avoids letter prev? Try all 26 letters; per letter jump straight to its leftmost occurrence at or after l and its rightmost occurrence at or before r; if those are two distinct spots, the value is 2 plus the recursive interior. Nearest-occurrence tables (or binary search over position lists) make each trial O(1) per letter.
s: Record the sorted positions of each letter.
dfs(l, r, prev): for each letter c different from prev, find li = leftmost occurrence of c in [l, r] and ri = rightmost occurrence.
If li < ri, candidate value is 2 + dfs(li + 1, ri - 1, c).
Memoize on (l, r, prev); windows shorter than two characters return 0.
Answer with dfs(0, n-1, sentinel letter).
a.t: O(26 * n^2) — each (window, prev-letter) state tries 26 letters in O(1) via occurrence tables
a.sp: O(26 * n^2) — memo table over windows and 27 possible prev values

a.n: Approach 2: Bottom-Up Interval DP with Max-Excluding-One
a.i: Fill dp[l][r][p] by iterating l downward and r upward so interior windows are always ready. The candidate value per letter depends only on (l, r), not on p - so compute the 26 candidates once per window, then produce every p in O(1) extra using prefix/suffix maxima. This removes a factor of 27 and eliminates recursion entirely.
s: Build nxt[l][c] / prv[r][c]: nearest occurrence tables on each side.
For each window l < r compute cand[c] = 2 + dp[li+1][ri-1][c] whenever li < ri.
dp[l][r][p] for p < 26 equals the maximum of cand excluding index p, obtained from prefix and suffix running maxima.
dp[l][r][26] (no ban yet) stores the plain maximum over cand.
a.t: O(26 * n^2) — candidates per window cost 26 steps and the exclusion trick is linear

w:
Say the edge-building insight out loud first; the third dimension (banned neighbor letter) is exactly what interviewers probe, since plain interval DP cannot enforce the adjacency rule.
Traps: allowing odd-length answers, forgetting that only the middle pair may repeat (so "aa" itself is a valid answer), and pairing a letter that occurs just once - the li < ri check prevents that.
Likely follow-ups: count good palindromic subsequences instead of finding the longest, or relax the adjacency rule to allow k equal neighbors.
